title: The dignity of work
hook: his hometown neighbors know Jesus by one thing: his trade

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus at the gate, and the preferential option for the poor. Your line was the poor first.

Who was Jesus to the people who grew up with him? In Mark, he comes home to Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue, and the neighbors can't get past one thing. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The Greek word is tekton, a builder, a craftsman. Whatever the crowds had seen, his own town knew him by his trade, by hands that cut and fit and carried. Catholic teaching takes that seriously: in Christ, God worked with his hands. Today, the dignity of work.
screen: `HOME TO NAZARETH.` → `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `GOD WORKED WITH HIS HANDS.`

segments.voice: First, work isn't a punishment. In Genesis, before anything has gone wrong, the Douay-Rheims says: "the Lord God took man, and put him into the paradise of pleasure, to dress it, and to keep it." Work is there in paradise. What comes after the fall is the sweat and the thorns: work made hard, not work invented. Second, work is for the person, not the person for work. John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on human work, and its center is this: the value of work comes first from the fact that the one doing it is a person. Scrubbing floors and running a company both carry the dignity of a human being at work. Nobody is only a cost on a spreadsheet. Third, workers have rights. Leo's Rerum Novarum told employers not to treat workers as things to make money from, and defended the right of workers to form their own associations. Later teaching names a just wage, safe conditions and rest, which the Church treats as rights, not favors. Fourth, rest belongs to work. The same Genesis that gives the garden gives the seventh day, when God rests. The Catechism calls the sabbath a protest against slavery to work and the worship of money. A day off isn't laziness in this teaching. It's a reminder that a person is more than an output.
screen: `WORK BEFORE THE FALL.` · `WORK IS FOR THE PERSON.` · `WORKERS HAVE RIGHTS.` · then, large: `REST BELONGS TO WORK.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you, a chair, a cup, the clothes you're wearing, and let the hands behind it come into view: someone built, grew, sewed, packed, drove, stocked, and most of them you'll never meet. Then pick one worker you will see today, a bus driver, a nurse, a mail carrier, a mechanic, and decide how you'll thank them, by name if you can, not for being nice but for the work. If you pray, you can pray for them.
The dignity of work. In Catholic teaching, work is part of how people were made, it exists for the person, and workers have rights. Today's word.
Your line: work has dignity. In this teaching, the one doing the work matters most. Rest well.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Joseph the Worker with a feast day, some dioceses offer a Labor Day Mass, and Catholic teaching on just wages and workers' associations is cited in debates about labor.

chat.who: a friend at the bus stop
chat.says: My job is just stocking shelves. Does the Church really think that work has dignity?
options: Yes. In this teaching the value of work comes first from the person doing it, whatever the task.
Only if it pays well; the Church measures work's dignity by the wage it brings in.
Only skilled work does; scrubbing floors has less dignity than running a company.
chat.meaning: John Paul the Second taught that work's value comes first from the person doing it; scrubbing floors and running a company share that dignity.

notes: Tekton glossed as 'a builder, a craftsman' (standard lexicon sense: a worker in wood, stone or metal). Confirm.
Rerum Novarum paragraph numbers vary between editions; confirm 20 (workers not to be treated as chattels) and 48–51 (workers' associations).
Laborem Exercens 6 paraphrased: the basis for the value of work is that the one doing it is a person. 'A whole letter on human work' is a description, not a count.
CCC 2172 paraphrased: the sabbath as a protest against the servitude of work and the worship of money.
